\chapter{Bread, Water, Wine}
\label{ch:food}
\hlchaptermodality{13}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name bread, water and wine in French, and ask for some of any of them.}

Three things on a table, and two opposite fates for one kind of word: aqua dissolved into eau, a single vowel spelled with three letters, while vīnum stayed legible in wine, vine and vinegar. pānis gave French its bread and English its companions. Then one rule that English simply leaves out — de plus the article, contracting to du — turns each noun from the thing into some of it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[le pain]{le pain — bread}

\label{lesson:FR-C11-pain}



\begin{quote}
Food at last. This one word sits at the centre of the French table, and it hides what may be the loveliest word-story English has.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{nasal-in} — the \textbf{-ain} is a \textbf{nasal vowel}: the air goes through the nose and the \textbf{n} is never said as a consonant of its own.
  \item \texttt{silent-final} — nothing after that vowel is pronounced.
  \item Together: \textbf{le pain} = \emph{luh PA(N)}, where the \emph{(n)} is the nose and not a letter you hear. It is masculine: \textbf{le} pain.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{pain} is Latin \textbf{pānis}, \textquotedblleft{}bread.\textquotedblright{} That much is unremarkable. What the root did in English is not.

Take \emph{com-}, \textquotedblleft{}with,\textquotedblright{} and put \emph{pānis} after it. \textbf{com + pānis} — \textquotedblleft{}one you break bread with.\textquotedblright{} That is a \textbf{companion}, and the word means nothing else:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{companion}, \textbf{company} — a \emph{company} was first a group who ate together, and only later a body of soldiers or a business
  \item \textbf{pantry} — the room the bread is kept in
  \item \textbf{pannier} — a bread-basket, now the bag slung over a bicycle or a donkey
\end{itemize}

So \emph{le pain} and \emph{companion} are the same root wearing two different jobs. French kept the bread; English kept the friendship built on it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}le pain\textquotedblright{} — \emph{luh PA(N)}, the vowel through the nose
  \item the sum — \textquotedblleft{}com + pānis: one you break bread with\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pain $\to$ companion, company, pantry\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}the bread\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{le pain}, \emph{luh PA(N)}.) Is the \textbf{n} a consonant here? (\textbf{No} — it marks the vowel as \textbf{nasal}.) What Latin word is it? (\textbf{pānis}.) What does \emph{companion} literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}One you \textbf{break bread with}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{com-} + \emph{pānis}.) Next: the drink that wore away to a single vowel.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[l'eau]{l'eau — water}

\label{lesson:FR-C11-eau}



\begin{quote}
Every word so far has been worn down a little. This one was worn down almost completely — and you can still hear what it used to be, in English.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{o-eau} — \textbf{eau} is pronounced \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}oh.\textquotedblright{}} That is the entire word. Three written letters, \emph{e-a-u}, spelling \textbf{one} vowel sound and nothing else.
  \item \texttt{elision} — it begins with a vowel sound, so the article elides: \textbf{l'eau}, not \emph{le eau}. The same elision you met on \textbf{l'été}.
  \item Together: \textbf{l'eau} = \emph{loh}. Two letters heard, four written.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{eau} is Latin \textbf{aqua}. Say those two aloud, one after the other, and the distance is almost comic.

Watch the erosion happen, though, and each step is small:

\emph{aqua} $\to$ \emph{ewe} $\to$ \emph{eaue} $\to$ \textbf{eau}

The \textbf{q} goes, then the \textbf{w}-sound goes, then the final vowel goes, and what is left is a held \textquotedblleft{}oh\textquotedblright{} with a spelling that remembers the rest. French, quite literally, \textbf{drank the consonants out of} \emph{aqua}.

Meanwhile the loud original survived — in \textbf{English}, which borrowed the Latin word whole and never wore it at all: \textbf{aqua}tic, \textbf{aqua}rium, \textbf{aque}duct, \textbf{aqua}lung. Italian barely touched it either: \emph{acqua}.

So \textbf{l'eau} and \textbf{aquarium} are the two far ends of one word, and English is holding the end that still looks like Latin.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}l'eau\textquotedblright{} — \emph{loh}, one vowel and no more
  \item the erosion — \textquotedblleft{}aqua, ewe, eaue, eau\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two ends — \textquotedblleft{}l'eau, aquarium\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}le pain, l'eau\textquotedblright{} — and notice why one elides and the other does not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}the water\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{l'eau}, \emph{loh}.) How many sounds are in \textbf{eau}? (\textbf{One.}) Why is the article \textbf{l'} and not \emph{le}? (\textbf{eau} begins with a \textbf{vowel sound}.) What Latin word is underneath it? (\textbf{aqua}.) Where can you still hear \emph{aqua} loud and whole? (\textbf{English} — \emph{aquatic}, \emph{aquarium}, \emph{aqueduct}; and Italian \emph{acqua}.) Next: the drink that refused to wear down.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[le vin]{le vin — wine}

\label{lesson:FR-C11-vin}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Eau} dissolved down to one vowel. This word, sitting on the same table, did the opposite — and the reason is not linguistic.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{nasal-in} — the same nasal you met in \textbf{pain}, spelled \textbf{-in} this time rather than \textbf{-ain}. Two spellings, one vowel.
  \item \texttt{silent-final} — again, the \textbf{n} is the nose and not a consonant.
  \item Together: \textbf{le vin} = \emph{luh VA(N)}. Say \textbf{pain} and \textbf{vin} back to back and hear that only the first consonant differs.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{vin} is Latin \textbf{vīnum} — and unlike \emph{aqua}, it is still recognisable everywhere it went.

English has it several times over, by several routes:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{wine} — \emph{vīnum} borrowed into early Germanic, long before French existed
  \item \textbf{vine}, \textbf{vine}yard — the plant it comes from
  \item \textbf{vin}egar — French \emph{vin} + \emph{aigre}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{sour wine},\textquotedblright{} which is exactly what vinegar is
  \item \textbf{vint}age, \textbf{vin}yl — the harvest year, and a plastic named from wine spirit
\end{itemize}

Why did \emph{aqua} dissolve while \emph{vīnum} held? Because words wear down with use and hold their shape when they are \textbf{traded}. Water is what you have; wine is what you buy, ship, tax and write down. A word that keeps appearing on a bill of lading in three countries stays legible in all three.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}le vin\textquotedblright{} — \emph{luh VA(N)}, the nose again
  \item the near-pair — \textquotedblleft{}le pain, le vin\textquotedblright{}; one consonant apart
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vin $\to$ wine, vine, vinegar\textquotedblright{}
  \item the contrast — \textquotedblleft{}l'eau wore away, le vin did not\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}the wine\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{le vin}, \emph{luh VA(N)}.) Which other word this chapter has the same vowel? (\textbf{le pain}.) What Latin word is behind it? (\textbf{vīnum}.) What does \emph{vinegar} literally say? (\textbf{Sour wine} — \emph{vin} + \emph{aigre}.) Next: how to ask for \textbf{some} of any of them.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[du pain, de l'eau]{du pain, de l'eau — asking for \emph{some}}

\label{lesson:FR-C11-du}



\begin{quote}
You have three things on the table and no way to ask for any of them yet. \textbf{le pain} is \emph{the} bread — a particular loaf. What you actually want at a table is \textbf{some} bread, and French makes you say so.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: French says \textquotedblleft{}of the\textquotedblright{}, where English says nothing}]
English can drop the word entirely. \emph{\textquotedblleft{}I'd like bread\textquotedblright{}} is perfectly good English. French cannot: it marks \textbf{an unmeasured amount of a thing} with \textbf{de} plus the article the noun already takes.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{de} + \textbf{le pain} $\to$ \textbf{du pain} — \emph{some bread}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{de} + \textbf{le vin} $\to$ \textbf{du vin} — \emph{some wine}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{de} + \textbf{l'eau} $\to$ \textbf{de l'eau} — \emph{some water}
\end{quote}

That is one rule, not three. \textbf{de + le} always contracts to \textbf{du}; \textbf{de + l'} has nothing to contract, so it simply stays apart. You are not learning a new list here — you are putting \emph{de} in front of the article you already know, and letting the vowel rule you already met decide the shape.

And the contrast is worth hearing directly:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{le pain} — \emph{the} bread, that loaf, the one on the table
  \item \textbf{un pain} — \emph{a} loaf, one whole item you could pick up
  \item \textbf{du pain} — \emph{some} bread, an amount with no edges
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three — \textquotedblleft{}du pain, du vin, de l'eau\textquotedblright{}
  \item the reason — \textquotedblleft{}de plus the article; du where it contracts\textquotedblright{}
  \item the ladder on one noun — \textquotedblleft{}le pain, un pain, du pain\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}du pain, du vin, de l'eau\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}some bread\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{du pain}.) Some wine? (\textbf{du vin}.) Some water? (\textbf{de l'eau} — \emph{eau} takes \textbf{l'}, so there is nothing to contract.) What are the two words hiding inside \textbf{du}? (\textbf{de} + \textbf{le}.) What is the difference between \emph{un pain} and \emph{du pain}? (\textbf{un pain} is \textbf{a loaf}, one whole item; \textbf{du pain} is \textbf{some bread}, an amount with no edges.) Next: all three together.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — the table, and asking for some of it}

\label{lesson:FR-C11-practice}



\begin{quote}
Three nouns and one rule. Run the nouns first, then put the rule on each of them in turn.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: the three, with their articles}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}le pain, l'eau, le vin\textquotedblright{}
  \item the odd one — \textquotedblleft{}l'eau elides, because it opens with a vowel\textquotedblright{}
  \item the near-pair — \textquotedblleft{}le pain, le vin\textquotedblright{}; the same nasal, one consonant apart
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}le pain, l'eau, le vin\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Your turn: now ask for some}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}du pain, du vin, de l'eau\textquotedblright{}
  \item each noun three ways — \textquotedblleft{}le pain, un pain, du pain\textquotedblright{}
  \item the same three ways for wine — \textquotedblleft{}le vin, un vin, du vin\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: two words that wore differently}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the erosion — \textquotedblleft{}aqua, ewe, eaue, eau\textquotedblright{}
  \item the survival — \textquotedblleft{}vīnum: wine, vine, vinegar\textquotedblright{}
  \item the sum — \textquotedblleft{}com plus pānis: companion\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{three nouns} you can put on a table, each with the right article.
  \item \textbf{one rule for \textquotedblleft{}some\textquotedblright{}} — \emph{de} plus the article, contracting to \textbf{du} where it can. It is the first time French has asked you to say something English simply leaves out.
  \item \textbf{two opposite fates for one kind of word.} \emph{aqua} dissolved into \emph{eau}; \emph{vīnum} is still legible in four English words. Everyday things wear down, traded things stay legible — which is a rule you can use on words you have not met yet.
  \item \textbf{a root that paid twice} — \emph{pānis} gave French its bread and English its \textbf{companions}.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give all three with their articles. (\textbf{le pain, l'eau, le vin}.) Why does only one of them elide? (\textbf{eau} begins with a \textbf{vowel sound}.) Ask for some of each. (\textbf{du pain, du vin, de l'eau}.) What two words are inside \textbf{du}? (\textbf{de} + \textbf{le}.) Which Latin word wore down to a single vowel, and which one barely moved? (\textbf{aqua} $\to$ \emph{eau}; \textbf{vīnum} $\to$ \emph{vin}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
